entity:meth_00232.name: Graph Neural Network for atomic property prediction in defective crystalline solids

selected.text: Including tensile strain as an input node feature enables the GNN to accurately predict stress evolution during loading, reproducing nonlinear strain‑stress curves for porous graphene.

In polycrystalline aluminum, the GNN predicts atomic potential energy with a mean normalized relative error of 11.0% (maximum ≈13%) and achieves R² = 0.99 for mean potential energy versus grain number.

The GNN framework generalizes across defect types (grain boundaries, vacancies) and material dimensionalities (2D graphene, 3D aluminum), and to unseen defect configurations in over 10⁶ porous graphene structures, maintaining high prediction accuracy despite being trained on only about 1,200 random samples.
The GNN predicts atomic tensile stress in porous graphene membranes under tensile strain with a mean normalized relative error of 4.9% and a maximum error of about 10%.

entity:meth_00140.name: Uncertainty-aware graph convolutional neural network for vibrational free‑energy prediction

selected.text: The presented workflow enables high‑throughput prediction of temperature‑induced solid‑solid phase transitions without performing explicit phonon calculations for each material, dramatically reducing computational cost.

A graph convolutional neural network predicts vibrational free energies with root‑mean‑square errors of 8.23 meV/atom (training), 11.34 meV/atom (validation) and 12.31 meV/atom (test), and its predictions for MgS and NaH polymorphs match DFT‑computed values across the 200–700 K range.

Screening of approximately 50 000 inorganic crystals with the machine‑learning model identified over 2 000 temperature‑induced solid‑solid polymorphic transitions between 300 K and 600 K, including 130 stable transitions within the technologically relevant 300 K–350 K interval.

Validation against experimental reports and independent first‑principles calculations confirms the robustness and predictive power of the ML‑guided framework, with reasonable agreement for transition temperatures of KNO₃, KNO₂ and CaCO₃, DFT‑calculated free‑energy differences matching ML predictions for a ten‑material subset, and thermal‑conductivity ratios for Li₄TiS₄ and NaNO₃ closely reproduced by DFT.

selected.text: A curated dataset of 476 binary ionic compound melting temperatures spanning 0-4,000°C was compiled for machine learning model development.

The two-step clustering approach provides interpretability by revealing different melting physics dominated by bonding types, with Cluster 1 governed by ionic bonding features and Cluster 2 by covalent bonding features.
Cohesive energy and elastic moduli (shear and bulk modulus) are the most important features for melting temperature prediction, as identified by both ensemble feature importance and SHAP analysis.
VS-SISSO symbolic regression generates interpretable expressions for melting temperature that provide qualitative insight into the melting physics dominating within each cluster.

entity:meth_00107.name: Comprehensive review of AI-driven multiscale modeling approaches for solid‑state physics and chemistry

selected.text: Graph neural network architectures such as MEGNet and SchNet enhance prediction of phase transitions, defect dynamics, and bulk material properties relative to classical computational approaches.

Machine‑learning‑driven interatomic potentials (e.g., GAP, DeePMD) and DFT‑trained surrogate models enable simulations of up to millions of atoms while retaining accuracy close to first‑principles benchmarks, making large‑scale high‑fidelity simulations feasible.

Neural‑network‑based electronic‑structure prediction tools achieve significant speedups over conventional density‑functional theory while maintaining comparable accuracy, accelerating electronic‑structure calculations.

Integrating renormalization‑group concepts with machine‑learning architectures has been used to predict transitions to canted antiferromagnetic phases in 3D Ising and Fermi‑Hubbard models, to classify quantum phases, and to recognize complex many‑body phases from raw simulation data.

entity:meth_00128.name: E(3)-equivariant Graph Neural Network for phase‑space integration

selected.text: The E(3)‑equivariant GNN surrogate provides superior accuracy compared with third‑ and fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature for thermal expansion of copper, martensitic phase transition of iron, and grain‑boundary energy calculations, matching molecular dynamics reference data.
Training the GNN on high‑fidelity Monte‑Carlo integration data enables accurate prediction of phase‑averaged energies and their derivatives for atomic clusters.
Standard Gaussian quadrature rules produce frame‑dependent (non‑objective) phase‑averaged internal energies for rotated crystal lattices.

Inference with the trained GNN is significantly faster than evaluating fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature, enabling frequent high‑dimensional integral evaluations and quasistatic finite‑temperature atomistic simulations without costly MD averaging.

Across nine MatBench structural property datasets, M3GNet yields lower mean absolute errors than MODNet, AtomSets‑V1, MEGNet, and AutoMatminer, with improvements of 20.5 %–41.3 % on large datasets such as perovskite formation energy and MP band gap, and demonstrates excellent prediction accuracy on the broader MatBench suite.

On the MD17 and MD17‑CCSD(T) molecular force‑field benchmarks, M3GNet achieves lower energy and force errors than the Embedded Atom Neural Network and comparable accuracy to state‑of‑the‑art message‑passing and equivariant neural networks; when benchmarked against quantum‑accurate CCSD/CCSD(T) data, it attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for several molecules.
A single universal M3GNet model trained simultaneously on six elements attains error metrics comparable to element‑specific M3GNet models.
The SevenNet machine-learned interatomic potential outperforms the earlier M3GNet model on the Matbench Discovery benchmark.
M3GNet is an extension of MEGNet model to include 3-body interactions, explicit atomic coordinates, and 3×3 crystal lattice matrix.
M3GNet achieves test mean absolute errors of 35 meV/atom for energy, 72 meV/Angstrom for force, and 0.41 GPa for stress.

selected.text: Inclusion of van der Waals interactions together with DFT+U improves the accuracy of predicted order‑disorder transition temperatures for LiCoO₂ relative to earlier first‑principles studies.

The AFLOW standard enables reproducible high-throughput DFT calculations through standardized parameter sets for k-point density, energy cut-offs, exchange-correlation functionals, pseudopotentials, DFT+U parameters, and convergence criteria.

A Hubbard U parameter of 2.5 eV in DFT+U (with a vdW‑DF exchange‑correlation functional) reproduces the experimental average lithiation voltages of LiCoO₂ across the composition ranges {0‑1}, {0‑0.5}, and {0.5‑1}.
The AFLOW Standard for High-Throughput Materials Science Calculations

M3GNet predicts phonon band structures and densities of states for SiO₂ polymorphs that quantitatively agree with DFT calculations, and the predicted phonon density‑of‑states center follows the expected ω ∝ 1/√m trend across materials.

The presented scale‑bridging framework, linking DFT‑informed statistical mechanics to continuum phase‑field models via IDNN‑learned free‑energy functions, constitutes the first systematic implementation of this kind for LiCoO₂ cathodes.

Predicting forces as the negative gradient of the learned total energy guarantees energy conservation and rotation‑equivariant forces.
Using higher-order E(3)-equivariant representations (increasing rotation order from l=0 to l=1 and up to l=3) consistently reduces prediction error and improves accuracy across all evaluated tasks.
The equivariant architecture scales linearly with the number of atoms because convolutions are limited to a local cutoff radius.
On the 3BPA molecule energy profile, MACE predictions are closest to the DFT ground truth across three dihedral slices, outperforming BOTNet and NequIP.

selected.text: Machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on OMat24 predict tightly converged DFT forces with accuracy comparable to or better than predictions for less tightly converged calculations.

MLIP models trained on OMat24 achieve F1 scores above 0.9 for stability prediction and 20 meV/atom accuracy for formation energy on Matbench Discovery, with all five top-performing models on the Matbench Discovery leaderboard exclusively trained on OMat24.

OMat24 comprises over 118 million DFT calculations across diverse chemistries, materials, and configurations for inorganic bulk materials, making it up to 2 orders of magnitude larger than other openly available datasets in terms of number of single-point calculations.

OMat24 exhibits more uniform and comprehensive coverage of near-neighbor pairs and element distributions compared to both Alexandria and MPtrj datasets, with elemental coverage spanning most of the periodic table.

Training a TensorNet model on the 400 k‑structure MatPES‑PBE dataset requires approximately 15 minutes per epoch on a single RTX A6000 GPU, whereas training on the 100 M‑structure OMat24 dataset needs about 20 hours per epoch on sixteen A100 GPUs, highlighting the computational efficiency of MatPES.
Rattled systems in the OMat24 dataset have deleterious effects on model performance when evaluated on out-of-distribution hetero-diatomic systems.

entity:meth_00144.name: Integrable Deep Neural Network (IDNN) for learning high‑dimensional free‑energy density and chemical potential functions

selected.text: The presented scale‑bridging framework, linking DFT‑informed statistical mechanics to continuum phase‑field models via IDNN‑learned free‑energy functions, constitutes the first systematic implementation of this kind for LiCoO₂ cathodes.

Integrable Deep Neural Networks trained on derivative (chemical‑potential) data accurately learn the high‑dimensional free‑energy density and chemical‑potential functions for LiₓCoO₂, achieving mean‑squared errors comparable to the reported minima and reproducing DFT formation energies with a mean absolute error below 5 meV atom⁻¹.

A cluster expansion fitted to 333 DFT‑computed LiCoO₂ configurations using a genetic‑algorithm‑guided sparse regression achieves a root‑mean‑square error of 2.49 meV per primitive cell under 10‑fold cross‑validation and accurately reproduces formation energies, especially for configurations on or near the convex hull.

Phase‑field simulations reproduce the lever‑rule mass fractions of ordered and disordered phases predicted by the Monte Carlo phase diagram after accounting for a slight shift in the order‑disorder boundaries from the IDNN free‑energy surface.

Using a shifted softplus activation guarantees an infinitely differentiable (smooth) potential energy surface, facilitating geometry optimization.

On the ISO17 benchmark, SchNet reaches chemical‑accuracy (≈0.5 kcal/mol MAE) for energy predictions on molecules seen during training and further improves predictions on unseen isomers when forces are included in training.
Graph neural network architectures such as MEGNet and SchNet enhance prediction of phase transitions, defect dynamics, and bulk material properties relative to classical computational approaches.

MEGNet models trained on approximately 60,000 crystals outperform prior models (SchNet and CGCNN) for formation energy, band gap, bulk modulus, and shear modulus, achieving errors comparable to or better than density‑functional‑theory uncertainties.
MEGNet models achieve lower mean absolute errors than SchNet on 11 of the 13 QM9 molecular properties evaluated.

selected.text: The computational cost of LiFlow scales linearly with the number of atoms (O(n)), in contrast to the cubic scaling (O(n³)) of ab initio molecular dynamics.
LiFlow predicts lithium mean‑squared displacement with a Spearman rank correlation of 0.7–0.8 on unseen material compositions, enabling screening of high‑diffusivity electrolytes.

LiFlow trained on 25 ps ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories can generate stable trajectories up to 1 ns in larger (4 × 4 × 4) supercells, reproducing lithium self‑diffusivity, activation energies, and temperature dependence comparable to long AIMD simulations.

A direct regression (Regressor) model yields higher mean‑squared‑displacement errors than the generative LiFlow model, demonstrating the necessity of generative modeling for accurate atomic transport simulation.
